sentences.text: The United Kingdom's role in the Allied Industrial Base is as a demand and market anchor: allies count on it more as a buyer of turbines, vehicles and reactor parts than as a supplier.
Its core seats in three strategic compacts are led by demand roles, and its main supply contribution is uranium conversion and enrichment.
Nationally, no producing step reaches the top quarter of producers, so nothing reads Preserve.

The industrial task is to catch up in the vehicle chain, where the anchors are, and to source battery cells and rare-earth materials from trusted partners, with development cooperation adding cell capacity now and preparing rare-earth capacity later.
Storage, wind and grid networks need to be built faster.
The high fence belongs around gas and oil supply, the rare-earth chain, and the control software of batteries and rooftop inverters.
Gas and oil supply, which is essential and imported and takes one to three years to rebuild; Norway alone provides 75% of gas imports.
The rare-earth chain, where China holds 94% of world refining supply.
The control software of battery systems and distributed PV inverters.
The answer is stocks, trusted supply and control of command paths, not self-sufficiency.
Catch Up in EV and charger manufacturing, EV drivetrain components and battery components.
Meet the high need for reactors mainly with allied makers, and keep conversion and enrichment reliable for allies.

Battery cells and packs from producers such as Poland, the United States and Hungary, and rare-earth and wind materials from Germany, Spain and Canada, where allied supply falls short; minerals from Australia, Canada and the United States.
With developing partners, add cell capacity now and prepare rare-earth capacity later.
Accelerate storage, wind power and grid networks, buying from trusted suppliers with security conditions on connected equipment.
Leave open grid components, oil refining, wafers and PV cells, gas-turbine equipment and the commodity mining steps.
In Figure 1, Secure sits in fuel extraction and rare-earth refining, Catch Up spreads across the manufacturing columns, and Partner covers minerals and battery cells.
The orange corner flags mark Secure software and magnet layers inside other steps.
Each cell is a supply-chain step of a technology, colored by its strategic choice.
A corner flag marks a mixed step whose named parts sit behind a different fence: in battery cells and packs, the battery software is Secure, the cells Partner and the enclosures Watch.
A dotted outline marks a review case, a call resting on low confidence, a review flag, a thin anchor or a known data artifact; this brief does not turn those calls into recommendations.
lack the data for a call.
Secure covers three whole steps and five layers inside other steps, grouped into four capabilities.
Gas and oil are Secure for system resilience, not coercion: they are essential, hard to substitute and slow to rebuild, though most imports come from suppliers not flagged as potentially coercive.
Supply-chain need is 92 out of a hundred; gas takes one to three years to rebuild.
Norway supplies 75% of imports; potentially coercive suppliers only 2%.
The risk is concentration and rebuild time.

Long-term and capacity-reservation contracts with trusted suppliers, such as Australia, the United States and Belgium (a list that can include trading hubs); stockholding obligations sized to the rebuild time; stress tests.
The rare-earth chain: separation, metals and magnets
Feeds the magnets of EV motors and wind generators; the United Kingdom holds 0% of world refining supply.
China holds 94% of world refining supply and trusted suppliers 4%.
Rebuilding takes more than three years.
New trusted capacity with allies such as Japan, Australia and the United States, through co-investment and offtake; at home only where announced projects can qualify; stockpiles until it qualifies.
Supply-chain need is 87; oil takes one to three years to rebuild.
Norway supplies 38% of imports; trusted suppliers hold 29% of world supply, and allied supply falls short.
Stocks sized to the rebuild time; capacity reservations with several trusted producers, such as Canada, the United States and Norway; demand-side substitution.
Control software of battery systems and PV inverters
Battery-management, energy-management and inverter firmware can command or disable storage and rooftop solar from abroad.
China supplies 61% of battery cell and pack imports and 23% of PV module and inverter imports: hardware shares, not software.
Trusted-source and certification rules for firmware, communications and remote access; limits on over-the-air updates by untrusted vendors; replacement of untrusted control in the installed base.
Grid, turbine, vehicle, and oil and gas control software mostly reads Watch.

The Secure software layers sit in the hardware bought most from potentially coercive suppliers: 66% of battery cell and pack imports and 27% of PV equipment, against 24% for transformers and switchgear.
These shares measure hardware, not software vendors, so basic security standards should still apply and the calls should be re-tested as suppliers change.
Medium fence — where industrial capability matters
There is no Preserve step, because no producing step reaches the top quarter of producers.
The highest positions, 63 in gas-turbine and drilling components and 63 in battery cells and packs (a Partner step with no capability anchor), sit below the bar of 75.

at deployment, Accelerate where deployment need reaches 60;

Preserve where Competitive Position is in the top quarter (75) and either Strategic Industrial Value (bar 60) or supply-chain need (bar 67) is high;
Catch Up where the value is high, the position is not, and a capability anchor is corroborated by other evidence;
Partner where supply-chain need is high but there is neither a top-quarter position nor, for a high-value step, a credible pathway;
Named layers inside a step, such as control software or magnets, take their own choice, and a step whose parts sit behind different fences is mixed.
